chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Harun ibn al-Jahm, from Ismail ibn Ammar al-Sayrafi, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'May I be sacrificed for you, a believer is a mercy upon a believer?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Yes.' I said, 'And how is that so?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Any believer who comes to his brother regarding a need, that is indeed a mercy from Allah sent to him and caused for him. So if he fulfills his need, he has accepted the mercy by accepting it; and if he turns him away from his need while he is able to fulfill it, he has turned away from himself a mercy from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent to him and caused for him.'

And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, hoards that mercy until the Day of Judgment, until the one who was turned away from his need becomes the judge over it. If he wills, he diverts it to himself, and if he wills, he diverts it to someone else. O Ismail! When it is the Day of Judgment and he is the judge over a mercy from Allah that has been initiated for him, to whom do you think he will divert it?' I said, 'I do not think he will divert it away from himself.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Do not guess, but be certain, for he will never turn it away from himself.'

O Ismail! The one whose brother comes to him regarding a need, him being able to fulfill it, but he does not fulfill it for him, Allah will cause a hydra to gnaw his big toe in his grave until the Day of Judgment, whether he is forgiven or punished.
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence of turning away a believer's need when one is able to help?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates that assisting a believer is a divine mercy actively bestowed by Allah, which is preserved in reserve until the Day of Judgment. The hadith introduces a unique eschatological mechanism where the beneficiary becomes the judge of this specific mercy, almost invariably retaining it for himself, thereby highlighting the spiritual risk of neglecting one's duty. This narrative underscores the concept of 'taqdir' (divine decree) intertwined with human agency, warning that failing to help a capable brother invites a specific grave punishment, whether one is ultimately forgiven or condemned.
